design_detail: Co-twin control analysis within a cross-sectional telephone diagnostic interview (1996–2000; the Semi-Structured Assessment for the Genetics of Alcoholism adapted for telephone use and DSM-IV) of the young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register (born 1964–1971; median age 30, range 24–36). The analysis uses 311 same-sex pairs (136 monozygotic, 175 dizygotic) in which one twin reported first cannabis use before age 17 and the co-twin did not (234 co-twins started at 17 or later, 77 never used cannabis). Outcomes: lifetime nonmedical use of sedatives, hallucinogens, cocaine/other stimulants and opioids; abuse/dependence on cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, opioids or any of them (modified criteria); DSM-IV alcohol dependence. Conditional logistic regression, unadjusted and adjusted for within-pair differences in covariates kept by backward stepwise selection; repeated in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis.
can_establish: That in Australian twins born 1964–1971 the twin who recalled starting cannabis before 17 more often reported later use of other drugs, drug abuse/dependence and alcohol dependence than the co-twin who did not, so that the association is not explained by everything co-twins share in their upbringing (and, for identical pairs, their genes).
cannot_establish: That early cannabis use caused the later outcomes: factors that differ between co-twins (peers, temperament, experiences) were measured only in part and retrospectively, the reported estimates pool fraternal pairs, who share about half their genes, without separate identical-pair estimates, and ages of first use were recalled at about 30.

sample.recruitment: Registry: young-adult cohort of the Australian Twin Register, a volunteer twin panel (pairs enrolled 1980–1982); a single telephone interview in 1996–2000 (p. 428, Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Same-sex pairs discordant for first cannabis use before 17: 311 of the 861 twins who started before 17 had such a co-twin. Seventeen individuals who reported starting sedatives (3), hallucinogens (6), stimulants (5) or opioids (3) before cannabis were excluded from the analyses (p. 428, Methods, 2nd paragraph; p. 430, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: 306 men (62 monozygotic and 91 dizygotic pairs) and 316 women (74 and 84 pairs); median age 30 (range 24–36). Early tobacco use (smoking at least weekly for 3 weeks or more before 17) in 36.6%; early regular drinking (at least monthly for 6 months or more before 17) in 11.6% (pp. 428–429).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); of 4,010 traceable pairs, both twins were interviewed in 2,765 (69% pairwise response) and one twin in another 735 (78% individual response) (p. 428, Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteer twin register with 69% pairwise response; the discordant pairs are a selected subset (311 pairs from 2,765 complete pairs); the concordance analysis lists more discordant same-sex pairs (407) than were analysed, unexplained (see reporting issues); handling of missing data is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported age at first cannabis use, asked earlier in the interview than drug problems to limit recall bias (p. 431, Comment, 2nd paragraph); early use = first use before 17. Zygosity from standard questions on physical similarity and confusion of the twins, which in earlier studies agreed with genotyping in more than 95% of pairs (p. 428).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured for the exposure: any use before 17, which the authors call a crude measure (p. 432, Comment, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Early tobacco and early regular alcohol use were measured and offered as covariates; people who started another illicit drug before cannabis were excluded.

comparison.controls: The co-twin from the same pair, who had not used cannabis before 17 (234 started later, 77 never used it).
comparison.matching: Matched by pair: same rearing household, sex and age for all pairs; all genes for monozygotic pairs and about half for dizygotic pairs. Within-pair covariate differences adjusted when retained by backward stepwise selection (P<.10).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Factors that differ between co-twins were measured only as lifetime conduct disorder, major depression, social anxiety, early tobacco and alcohol use (and, per the abstract, parental conflict/separation and childhood sexual abuse), all recalled at about 30, without establishing that they came before cannabis use; peer affiliation and temperament were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Most co-twins (234 of 311) used cannabis after 17; Table 3 repeats the analysis in pairs in which both twins used cannabis.

outcomes.instruments: Telephone-adapted Semi-Structured Assessment for the Genetics of Alcoholism (DSM-IV): lifetime nonmedical use of each drug class; for classes used at least monthly, abuse (either of 2 abuse symptoms) and dependence (2 or more of 4 dependence symptoms), modified rather than formal DSM-IV criteria; alcohol dependence by full DSM-IV criteria (pp. 428–429).
outcomes.validity_norms: The modified cannabis dependence criteria had sensitivity 96.7% and specificity 94.6% against DSM-IV in an earlier analysis of this sample (p. 429).
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime outcomes reported at a median age of 30; drug classes combined for abuse/dependence because of low prevalence.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 95% confidence intervals for 10 outcomes in two samples; power was computed at the .01 level (pp. 429–430).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; whether interviewers knew the co-twin's answers is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Conditional odds ratios, twin who started cannabis before 17 against co-twin (311 pairs, Table 2): unadjusted 2.83 (95% CI 1.66–4.85) sedative use, 5.15 (2.85–9.33) hallucinogen use, 4.19 (2.60–6.75) cocaine/stimulant use, 2.57 (1.39–4.77) opioid use; 2.13 (1.45–3.13) cannabis, 2.67 (0.71–10.05) sedative, 4.13 (1.91–8.93) cocaine/stimulant, 3.67 (1.02–13.14) opioid and 2.24 (1.52–3.30) any drug abuse/dependence; 2.17 (1.46–3.24) alcohol dependence. Adjusted: 2.28, 5.15, 4.06, 2.34; 1.96, 2.67, 3.98, 3.67, 1.98; 1.85. Absolute differences in lifetime prevalence (editors' calculation from Table 2): cocaine/stimulant use 47.9% against 26.4% (21.5 points), hallucinogen use 17.4 points, any drug abuse/dependence 14.8 points, alcohol dependence 13.2 points, opioid use 7.1 points. Editors' reconstruction of the discordant pairs from the printed prevalences reproduces every unadjusted odds ratio and interval (for example 67 against 13 pairs for hallucinogen use; 8 against 3 for sedative abuse/dependence).
analysis.covariates: Within-pair differences in early regular tobacco use, early regular alcohol use, conduct disorder, major depression and social anxiety (and, per the abstract, parental conflict/separation and childhood sexual abuse), retained by backward stepwise selection at P<.10 with early cannabis use forced in (p. 429, Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 2 footnote).
analysis.selective_reporting: Separate monozygotic and dizygotic analyses and alternative cut-offs (before 15, 16 and 18) are described only as confirming the conclusions, without estimates; the zygosity and sex interactions are reported only as P>.10 (p. 429; p. 431, Subsidiary Analyses).
analysis.power: By simulation at the .01 level: 80% or more for odds ratios above 1.7 for five outcomes and above 2.5 for sedative use, opioid use and cocaine/stimulant abuse/dependence; low for sedative and opioid abuse/dependence (pp. 429–430). The printed formula for the minimum odds ratio is not an odds ratio (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within 311 same-sex pairs, the twin who recalled starting cannabis before 17 more often reported later use of each other drug class (conditional odds ratios 2.6 to 5.2), drug abuse/dependence (2.1 to 4.1; sedatives not significant) and alcohol dependence (2.2) than the co-twin. Adjusting for within-pair differences in measured covariates lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth (to 1.9–5.2). In the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis the unadjusted odds ratios were 1.6 to 6.0, and after adjustment cannabis abuse/dependence (P=.06) and sedative abuse/dependence were no longer significant. No identical-pair estimates are shown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the associations cannot be explained solely by shared genetic or environmental predisposition and suggests that they may arise from the peer and social context in which cannabis is used and obtained, lowering perceived barriers to and giving access to other drugs (p. 427); the Comment says the results are consistent with a causal role and that heritable factors cannot explain the association because identical pairs share their genes (p. 431). The shared-environment conclusion is supported; the genetic one rests on identical pairs whose separate estimates are not reported (only a non-significant interaction, with 136 identical pairs), while more than half of the pairs analysed are fraternal. Factors that differ between co-twins are judged less plausible rather than measured. The abstract calls the effect of adjustment 'negligible', though the odds ratios fell by up to about a fifth. The proposed mechanisms (peer context, lowered perceived risk, access through dealers, pharmacological sensitization) are not tested. The Comment itself says strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from these associations alone (p. 432).

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the sequence behind the gateway question (see that card).

Grant & Dawson, US national survey: earlier age at first drug use went with DSM-IV drug abuse and dependence; cited here among non-twin studies reporting early onset as a risk factor (card written in the same round).

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a model with a shared propensity and no gateway effect reproduces the population-level gateway phenomena; it does not address comparisons within twin pairs (see that card).

Wagner & Anthony: in US household surveys, marijuana use went with an earlier first chance to try cocaine and with starting it once offered, in line with the access mechanism proposed here (see that card).
This study, with an editorial (JAMA 289(4):482–483; PubMed 12533129) and, later in 2003, four letters with the authors' reply (JAMA 290(3):329–332; PubMed 12865366–12865369), none read for this card.

Irons, Iacono & McGue, Minnesota twins: drinking by 14 went with more drug classes used at 24 within identical pairs discordant for early drinking, a co-twin result for alcohol rather than cannabis (as recorded on that card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication of this co-twin result for cannabis appears in the sources read for this card, and the editorial and letters were not available; later studies were not searched by this reader. The authors note that the association with early cannabis use had been reported in prospective non-twin studies (references 16–19, not read). Among the gateway papers of this round it is the design that best controls shared family factors; the reading list notes that no study separates the causal, common-liability and availability explanations in one design.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest or financial-disclosure statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Queensland Institute of Medical Research; Missouri Alcoholism Research Center and Departments of Psychiatry (Washington University School of Medicine) and Psychology (University of Missouri) (p. 427).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective twin study that records cannabis use, peer affiliation and behaviour problems in both twins from before first use through adolescence, reports identical-pair estimates separately with enough discordant identical pairs to be precise, and dates later drug use; replicated in another country with different cannabis availability.

domains.note: The pair design removes shared rearing environment and, in identical pairs, genes; but the reported estimates pool fraternal pairs (56% of pairs) without separate identical-pair estimates, and factors that differ between co-twins (peers, temperament) were not measured, with the covariates used recalled at about 30 and chosen by stepwise selection, some possibly consequences rather than causes of early use.

Age at first cannabis use recalled at a median age of 30 with a cut-off at 17; 234 of 311 co-twins also used cannabis, so many pairs may differ by a year or two near the cut-off; recall could be shaped by later drug involvement.
Volunteer register with 69% pairwise response; 311 discordant pairs analysed against 407 listed in the concordance analysis, unexplained.
Missing answers and the handling of the 17 people excluded for using another drug before cannabis are not described; the table percentages use all 311 (234) pairs.
Lifetime outcomes self-reported in the same interview as the exposure, using modified abuse/dependence criteria for drugs; interviewer blinding not reported.
All 10 outcomes are reported unadjusted and adjusted, but identical-pair and alternative cut-off analyses are summarized without estimates, and one adjusted row of Table 3 duplicates Table 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The co-twin comparison holds constant everything co-twins share in their upbringing and, for identical pairs, their genes, which none of the other gateway designs of this round can do, so it is the strongest of them on confounding. It still cannot exclude factors that differ between co-twins, the estimates pool fraternal pairs with no identical-pair results shown, and early use was recalled in adulthood. Citable for the within-pair associations (Table 2) as evidence that shared family environment does not account for the link between early cannabis use and later drug use in this Australian cohort; not as proof that early cannabis use causes later drug use, and not for the mechanisms proposed.

key_findings.finding: Of 4,010 traceable pairs, both twins were interviewed in 2,765 (69% pairwise response) and one twin in 735 (78% individual response), 6,265 people in all; 3,772 had used cannabis, 861 (13.7%) before 17; 311 of these (36.1%) had a same-sex co-twin who had not used cannabis before 17 (234 started later, 77 never), giving 622 twins.
The 311 discordant pairs comprised 74 female and 62 male identical pairs and 84 female and 91 male same-sex fraternal pairs; median age 30 (range 24–36).

In the full interview sample, concordance for cannabis use before 17 was higher in identical than fraternal pairs: men 65 concordant and 88 discordant identical pairs against 59 and 110 fraternal (chi-square 7.92, 1 df, P=.005); women 61 and 98 against 44 and 111 (chi-square 7.80, P=.005); the authors read this as heritable influence on age at first cannabis use.
key_findings.note: The test is a Breslow-Day comparison whose full counts (pairs concordant for no early use) are not printed, so it cannot be recomputed; the discordant counts here exceed the 311 pairs analysed (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Lifetime prevalence, twin who started cannabis before 17 against co-twin: sedative use 19.0% against 8.4%; hallucinogen use 35.4% against 18.0%; cocaine/stimulant use 47.9% against 26.4%; opioid use 13.5% against 6.4%; cannabis abuse/dependence 45.7% against 31.8%; cocaine/stimulant abuse/dependence 12.5% against 4.5%; any drug abuse/dependence 47.6% against 32.8%; alcohol dependence 42.8% against 29.6%.
key_findings.note: Absolute differences (editors' calculation): 21.5 points for cocaine/stimulant use, 17.4 for hallucinogens, 14.8 for any drug abuse/dependence, 13.2 for alcohol dependence, 7.1 for opioid use.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted conditional odds ratios (311 pairs): sedative use 2.83 (95% CI 1.66–4.85), hallucinogen use 5.15 (2.85–9.33), cocaine/stimulant use 4.19 (2.60–6.75), opioid use 2.57 (1.39–4.77); cannabis abuse/dependence 2.13 (1.45–3.13), sedative 2.67 (0.71–10.05), cocaine/stimulant 4.13 (1.91–8.93), opioid 3.67 (1.02–13.14), any drug 2.24 (1.52–3.30); alcohol dependence 2.17 (1.46–3.24). All but sedative abuse/dependence were significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, unadjusted conditional OR column; Results, items 1 and 2
key_findings.note: Editors' reconstruction from the printed prevalences (pairs in which only the early-use twin, or only the co-twin, had the outcome) reproduces each odds ratio and interval, for example 67 against 13 pairs for hallucinogen use, 88 against 21 for cocaine/stimulant use, 83 against 37 for any drug abuse/dependence and 8 against 3 for sedative abuse/dependence.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for within-pair differences in the covariates retained (P<.10): sedative use 2.28 (1.20–4.31), hallucinogen use 5.15 (2.85–9.33, no covariate retained), cocaine/stimulant use 4.06 (2.30–7.17), opioid use 2.34 (1.13–4.85); cannabis abuse/dependence 1.96 (1.25–3.09), sedative 2.67 (0.71–10.05), cocaine/stimulant 3.98 (1.73–9.17), opioid 3.67 (1.02–13.14), any drug 1.98 (1.26–3.10); alcohol dependence 1.85 (1.21–2.83). Early regular tobacco and alcohol use were the covariates most often retained; 9 of 10 outcomes remained significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, adjusted columns and footnote; Results, item 3 and 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis (54 female and 53 male identical, 56 female and 71 male fraternal), unadjusted odds ratios were 3.00 (1.60–5.62) sedative use, 3.92 (2.13–7.21) hallucinogen use, 3.00 (1.83–4.92) cocaine/stimulant use, 2.33 (1.19–4.59) opioid use; 1.58 (1.05–2.37) cannabis, 6.00 (0.72–49.83) sedative, 4.29 (1.88–9.76) cocaine/stimulant, 5.00 (1.10–22.82) opioid and 1.75 (1.16–2.64) any drug abuse/dependence; 2.03 (1.30–3.17) alcohol dependence. After adjustment, cannabis abuse/dependence was 1.57 (0.98–2.52; P=.06) and sedative abuse/dependence was not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Analyses Restricted to Those Reporting Lifetime Cannabis Use (p. 430, continuing p. 431); Table 3 (p. 431)

key_findings.finding: Interactions of early cannabis use with zygosity and with sex were not significant (P>.10 in all cases), so the data were pooled; separate identical- and fraternal-pair analyses with early use defined as before 15, 16 or 18 are said to confirm the conclusions, without estimates.
Abuse/dependence by sex in the 622 twins: cannabis 50.0% of men and 27.9% of women; any illicit drug 51.3% and 29.4%; cocaine/stimulants 11.8% and 5.4%; alcohol dependence 44.8% and 27.9%.

The modified cannabis dependence criteria had sensitivity 96.7% and specificity 94.6% against DSM-IV in an earlier analysis of this sample; 36.6% of twins in the discordant pairs reported early tobacco use and 11.6% early regular drinking.
key_findings.locator: Lifetime Drug Abuse/Dependence; Family, Social, and Individual Factors › Early Tobacco Use; Early Regular Alcohol Use

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the results consistent with early cannabis use having a causal role, consider unshared environmental influences less plausible because co-twins grew up in the same household, and argue that family background or heritable factors cannot explain the association.

Limitations and counter-arguments given by the authors: reliance on retrospective self-report and no data on ages at progression to frequent use or problems; age at first use was asked before drug problems; under-reporting by one twin is judged implausible because some cannabis use was normative in this cohort; delayed onset in co-twins is judged unlikely because more than 95% of people in the sample who used cannabis had started by 24.

Mechanisms offered if the association is causal, none tested here: pharmacological sensitization (supported only by rat studies, which the authors note used larger exposures than early use involves), pleasurable early experiences, lowered perceived risk of legal sanctions, and access to other drugs through dealers. The authors state that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from these associations alone.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 (234 pairs) the adjusted odds ratio for alcohol dependence, 1.85 (1.21–2.83) with covariates 3 and 4, is identical to the Table 2 value (311 pairs), although the samples and the unadjusted odds ratios differ (2.03 against 2.17).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably duplicated in error; the adjusted alcohol-dependence estimate for the restricted sample is unknown and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The power calculation defines the minimum odds ratio as pE(1−pE)/pU(1−pU), which is not an odds ratio. With the stated pE = 12.5% and pU = 4.5% it gives 2.5 (editors' calculation), the threshold the paper reports for cocaine/stimulant abuse/dependence, whereas the odds ratio for those prevalences is 3.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: The power statements may refer to a misdefined quantity, so the power to detect the stated odds ratios is uncertain; the main results are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The concordance analysis lists 407 same-sex pairs discordant for cannabis use before 17 (88 + 110 male, 98 + 111 female, 186 of them identical), whereas the analysis uses 311 pairs (136 identical); the difference is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: About a quarter of the discordant pairs, including 50 identical pairs, are missing from the analysis for unstated reasons, which could matter for the identical-pair argument.

reporting_issues.issue: Denominators: the 17 people who started another drug before cannabis are said to be excluded, yet the prevalences in Tables 2 and 3 use all 311 and 234 pairs; the sex-specific prevalences of use in the Methods imply slightly smaller denominators than 306 men and 316 women; and the 24.8% described as twins in discordant pairs who never used cannabis is 77 of the 311 co-twins (12.4% of the 622 twins).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; which analyses excluded the 17 people is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment's ranges (2.3- to 3.9-fold for other drug use, 1.6- to 6.0-fold for alcohol dependence and drug abuse/dependence) come from the unadjusted odds ratios of the restricted sample (Table 3), include the non-significant sedative abuse/dependence estimate (6.00, 0.72–49.83), and are said to hold whether or not pairs were identical, though no identical-pair estimates are shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should use the Table 2 estimates; the statement about identical pairs rests on a non-significant interaction test, not on shown estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists parental conflict/separation and childhood sexual abuse among the covariates controlled, and the Methods say the family-environment and abuse measures are described below, but the covariate section describes only psychiatric disorders, social anxiety, early tobacco use and early regular alcohol use.
reporting_issues.consequence: How those two covariates were measured and entered is not described in this paper; they were never retained by the stepwise selection.
